notes.meaning: Paul explains why he changed his travel plans and delayed his trip to Corinth. A previous visit had brought intense grief and sharp confrontation. He chose to stay away for a time so he would not bring them another sorrowful visit before they had time to repent.

Paul points out how deeply his own joy is tied to the Corinthian believers. If he arrived only to rebuke them and make them sad, the very people who were meant to cheer his heart would be in tears. He wanted to give them space to make things right so their reunion could be joyful.

Paul explains why he wrote a stern letter instead of visiting in person. He wanted them to correct their faults before he arrived, sparing both them and himself from heartbreak. He was confident that when they were truly happy in the Lord, he would share in their joy as well.

Paul reveals how deeply it pained him to write that corrective letter. He did not write out of cold anger, but with intense anguish and many tears. His true motive was not to cause them grief, but to prove how much he genuinely loved them.

Paul gently addresses the man whose wrongdoing had caused so much trouble in the church. The hurt was not done to Paul alone, but had brought shame and sorrow to the entire congregation. Paul is careful not to exaggerate the injury or place too heavy a burden on everyone.

The church discipline carried out by the majority of the congregation had accomplished its goal. Church discipline means removing an unrepentant person from church fellowship to help them see their sin. Because the man had repented, the punishment had done its work and needed to go no further.

differ.view: Baptists understand the punishment by the majority as proof that church discipline belongs to the whole local congregation rather than to a single bishop or ruling council.

notes.meaning: Paul urges the believers to switch from correcting the offender to forgiving and comforting him. If the church continued to shut him out, the man might drown in hopeless sorrow. True Christian correction always seeks to heal and restore the fallen, never to destroy them.

Paul pleads with the church to publicly and warmly welcome the repentant man back into their fellowship. Just as their rebuke had been open and clear, their love needed to be just as visible. Reaffirming love removes all doubt that a brother is fully received again.

Paul writes that his earlier instructions had been a test of the church's spiritual maturity. He wanted to see if they would follow God's guidance in every circumstance. Having proved obedient in carrying out necessary discipline, they now had to prove obedient in showing mercy.

Paul readily joins the Corinthians in extending full pardon to the repentant brother. He grants this forgiveness in the presence and authority of Christ for the benefit of the church. When believers forgive together, peace and unity are preserved in the body of Christ.

Paul warns that an unforgiving spirit gives Satan a prime opportunity to outwit the church. The devil's schemes involve tempting churches either to overlook sin or to become so harsh that sinners give up in despair. Christians must stay alert so they do not fall into these traps.

Paul describes his journey to the city of Troas to preach the gospel, the good news about Jesus. The Lord provided a wonderful opening for people to hear and respond to the message. Even though the door was open, Paul remained deeply concerned about how things were going in Corinth.

Paul could not find rest in his spirit because his partner Titus had not yet arrived with news from Corinth. His love and anxiety for the Corinthians were so strong that he left the open field at Troas. He crossed over into Macedonia, hoping to meet Titus on the road.

Paul breaks into praise to God, who always leads His servants in Christ's victory. He pictures a Roman victory parade, where sweet incense filled the streets as the general marched through. Wherever God leads His ministers, He uses them to spread the pleasing knowledge of Christ everywhere.

differ.view: Charismatics often emphasize that believers march as officers and co-victors sharing actively in the triumph of Christ.
Reformed Christians often view believers as willing captives whom Christ has conquered and displays as trophies of His sovereign grace.

notes.meaning: Paul explains that faithful ministers are like a sweet perfume of Christ pleasing to God. This aroma goes out among both groups of people in the world: those who are being saved and those who are perishing. God is pleased with the faithful proclamation of Christ regardless of how people respond.

To those who reject Christ, the gospel message smells like the stench of death leading to condemnation. To those who believe, it smells like a delightful fragrance leading to eternal life. Faced with such eternal stakes, Paul asks who could ever be worthy or qualified on their own for such a task.

Paul contrasts his team with dishonest teachers who peddle and water down God's word for personal gain. Like dishonest wine merchants who dilute their drinks to make money, false teachers compromised the truth. Paul and his companions preached with pure sincerity, speaking in Christ right under the watchful eye of God.
